title: Watermelon
descriptionHtml:
One hot summer day Pete and his friend Billy decided to buy a watermelon. They chose the biggest and the ripest one, in their opinion. After that the watermelon was weighed, and the scales showed $w$ kilos.

They rushed home, dying of thirst, and decided to divide the berry, however they faced a hard problem.

Pete and Billy are great fans of even numbers, that's why they want to divide the watermelon in such a way that each of the two parts weighs an even number of kilos, at the same time it is not obligatory that the parts are equal.

The boys are extremely tired and want to start their meal as soon as possible, that's why you should help them and find out, if they can divide the watermelon in the way they want. For sure, each of them should get a part of positive weight.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first (and the only) input line contains integer number $w$ ($1 \le w \le 100$) — the weight of the watermelon bought by the boys.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print YES, if the boys can divide the watermelon into two parts, each of them weighing even number of kilos; and NO in the opposite case.
sampleNotesHtml: For example, the boys can divide the watermelon into two parts of $2$ and $6$ kilos respectively (another variant — two parts of $4$ and $4$ kilos).
hints: Both parts must be even positive integers: part1 >= 2 and part2 >= 2.
The sum of two even numbers is always even. So if w is odd, it's impossible!
Beware of small even numbers: what happens when w = 2? The only positive division is 1 + 1, but 1 is odd!
explanation: For the watermelon to be split into two positive even integers, say $2k$ and $2m$, the total weight must be $w = 2k + 2m = 2(k+m)$, which is even. Furthermore, since $k \ge 1$ and $m \ge 1$, $w \ge 4$. Therefore, any even number strictly greater than 2 can be split into $2$ and $w - 2$. Hence, answer is YES if $w > 2$ and $w \% 2 == 0$, else NO.

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: Even Weight 8
testCases.description: Official sample test: 8 can be divided into 2 + 6 or 4 + 4.

testCases.title: Edge Case: Minimum Even Weight 2
testCases.description: Critical edge case: 2 can only be split into 1 and 1, neither of which is even.

testCases.title: Odd Weight: 7
testCases.description: An odd number cannot be the sum of two even numbers.

testCases.title: Maximum Constraint: 100
testCases.description: Upper bound test case: 100 is even and > 2 (e.g. 50 + 50).

title: Way Too Long Words
descriptionHtml:
Sometimes some words like "localization" or "internationalization" are so long that writing them many times in one text is quite tiresome.

Let's consider a word too long, if its length is strictly more than 10 characters. All too long words should be replaced with a special abbreviation.

This abbreviation is made like this: we write down the first and the last letter of a word and between them we write the number of letters between the first and the last letters. That number is in decimal system and doesn't contain any leading zeroes.

Thus, "localization" will be spelt as "l10n", and "internationalization" will be spelt as "i18n".

You are suggested to automatize the process of changing the words with abbreviations. At that all too long words should be replaced by the abbreviation and the words that are not too long should not undergo any changes.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains an integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 100$). Each of the following $n$ lines contains one word. All the words consist of lowercase Latin letters and possess lengths from $1$ to $100$ characters.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print $n$ lines. The $i$-th line should contain the result of replacing of the $i$-th word from the input data.
sampleNotesHtml: For a word of length $\le 10$, output it as is. For a word of length $> 10$, abbreviation is word[0] + (length - 2) + word[last].
hints: Check length: is length strictly greater than 10? (> 10, not >= 10).
If length <= 10, print the word untouched.
The abbreviation formula is: word[0] + (word.length - 2) + word[word.length - 1].
explanation: Iterate through each word. Check its character length. If length is greater than 10, format as the first char, the number (length - 2), and the last char. Otherwise output the original word.

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: Mixed Lengths
testCases.description: Official sample with short words and extremely long words.

testCases.title: Boundary Test: Exact Length 10
testCases.description: Words with exactly 10 letters must NOT be abbreviated.

testCases.title: Boundary Test: Length 11
testCases.description: Words with 11 letters are the smallest to be abbreviated (11 - 2 = 9).

testCases.title: Long Words With Repeating Letters
testCases.description: Words with identical start and end letters.

title: Team
descriptionHtml:
One day three best friends Petya, Vasya and Tonya decided to form a team and take part in programming contests. Participants are usually offered several problems during programming contests. Long before the start the friends decided that they will implement a problem if at least two of them are sure about the solution. Otherwise, the friends won't write the problem's solution.

This contest offers $n$ problems to the participants. For each problem we know, which friend is sure about the solution. Help the friends find the number of problems for which they will write a solution.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first input line contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 1000$) — the number of problems in the contest. Then $n$ lines contain three integers each, each integer is either $0$ or $1$. If the first number in the line equals $1$, then Petya is sure about the problem's solution, otherwise he isn't sure. The second number shows Vasya's view on the solution, the third number shows Tonya's view. The numbers on the lines are separated by spaces.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the number of problems the friends will implement on the contest.
sampleNotesHtml: In the first sample, Petya and Vasya are sure on problem 1, all three are sure on problem 2, and only Petya on problem 3. Total solved = 2.
hints: For each problem, sum up the three values: Petya + Vasya + Tonya.
If the sum is >= 2, increment your answer counter.
Print the final total count.
explanation: For each problem, check whether at least two friends are confident (i.e. $a + b + c \ge 2$). If yes, increment the answer.

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: 3 Problems
testCases.description: Official sample 1: two problems have >= 2 confident friends.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: 2 Problems
testCases.description: Official sample 2: one problem has >= 2 confident friends.

testCases.title: No Agreement: All Single Votes
testCases.description: Problems where at most 1 friend is sure.

testCases.title: Unanimous Agreement
testCases.description: All 3 friends agree on all problems.

title: Next Round
descriptionHtml:
"Contestant who earns a score equal to or greater than the $k$-th place finisher's score will advance to the next round, as long as the contestant earns a positive score..." — an excerpt from contest rules.

A total of $n$ participants took part in the contest ($n \ge k$), and you already know their scores. Calculate how many participants will advance to the next round.
inputSpecificationHtml:
The first line of the input contains two integers $n$ and $k$ ($1 \le k \le n \le 50$) separated by a single space.

The second line contains $n$ space-separated integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ ($0 \le a_i \le 100$), where $a_i$ is the score earned by the participant who got the $i$-th place. The given sequence is non-increasing (that is, for all $i$ from $1$ to $n - 1$ the following condition is fulfilled: $a_i \ge a_{i+1}$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Output the number of participants who advance to the next round.
sampleNotesHtml:
In the first sample the participant on the 5th place earned 7 points. As the participant on the 6th place also earned 7 points, there are 6 advancers.

In the second sample nobody got a positive score (score > 0), so 0 advance.
hints: Find the score of the k-th participant: remember in 0-indexed arrays, this is scores[k - 1].
A participant qualifies if score >= scores[k - 1] AND score > 0.
Even if a participant ties with the k-th place, their score must be strictly greater than 0!
explanation: Read $n$ and $k$. The cutoff score is $scores[k-1]$. Count all scores $s$ such that $s \ge scores[k-1]$ and $s > 0$.

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: Tie at Cutoff
testCases.description: Official sample 1: 5th and 6th place tie with 7 points.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: All Zero Scores
testCases.description: Official sample 2: positive score rule eliminates everyone.

testCases.title: All Qualify
testCases.description: All participants have identical positive score.

testCases.title: Cutoff is Zero
testCases.description: Participants after index with positive score qualify.

title: Domino piling
descriptionHtml:
You are given a rectangular board of $M \times N$ squares. You are also given an unlimited number of standard domino pieces of $2 \times 1$ squares.

You are asked to place as many dominoes as possible on the board so as to meet the following conditions:

  1. Each domino completely covers two squares.
  2. No two dominoes overlap.
  3. Each domino lies entirely inside the board. It is allowed to touch the edges of the board.

Find the maximum number of dominoes, which can be placed under these restrictions.
inputSpecificationHtml: In a single line you are given two integers $M$ and $N$ ($1 \le M \le N \le 16$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Output one number — the maximal number of dominoes, which can be placed.
sampleNotesHtml: Each domino covers exactly 2 squares. The board has $M \times N$ squares. Maximum dominoes is $\lfloor (M \times N) / 2 \rfloor$.
hints: Total squares on the board = M * N.
Each domino covers exactly 2 squares.
Can we always tile all squares except 1 if total area is odd? Yes! The formula is simply floor((M * N) / 2).
explanation: Because a domino covers 2 squares, at most $\lfloor \frac{M \cdot N}{2} \rfloor$ dominoes can be placed. Standard greedy strip-filling confirms this upper bound is always achievable.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: 3 x 3 Board
testCases.description: Official sample 2: 3 * 3 = 9 squares, fits 4 dominoes with 1 leftover square.

testCases.title: Single 1 x 1 Square
testCases.description: A 1x1 board cannot fit even one 2x1 domino.

title: Bit++
descriptionHtml:
The classic programming language of Bitland is Bit++. A language that is so peculiar and complicated.

The language is that peculiar as it has only one variable, called $x$. Also, there are two operations:

  • Operation ++ increases the value of variable $x$ by 1.
  • Operation -- decreases the value of variable $x$ by 1.

A statement in language Bit++ is a sequence, consisting of exactly one operation and one variable $x$. The statement is written without spaces, that is, it can only contain characters +, -, X. Executing a statement means applying its operation to variable $x$.

A programme in Bit++ is a sequence of statements, each of them needs to be executed. Putting values to variable $x$ is called executing the programme. Initially the value of $x$ is 0.

You are given a programme in Bit++. Execute it and find the final value of variable $x$.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains a single integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 150$) — the number of statements in the programme. Next $n$ lines contain statements. Each line contains exactly one statement. The statements are valid Bit++ statements: ++X, X++, --X, or X--.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the final value of $x$.
sampleNotesHtml: If the statement contains '+', $x$ increases by 1. If it contains '-', $x$ decreases by 1.
hints: The variable starts at 0.
Notice that every operation contains either '+' or '-'. If it contains '+', x = x + 1, otherwise x = x - 1.
The position of X (prefix vs postfix) doesn't change the final accumulator value.
explanation: Start with $x = 0$. For each instruction, check if it contains the character '+'. If so, increment $x$ by 1. Otherwise decrement $x$ by 1. Return the final value.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: Balanced Operations
testCases.description: Official sample 2: X++ then --X returns to 0.

title: Petya and Strings
descriptionHtml:
Little Petya loves presents. His mum bought him two strings of the same size for his birthday. The strings consist of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters. Now Petya wants to compare those two strings lexicographically.

The letters' case does not matter, that is an uppercase letter is considered equivalent to the corresponding lowercase letter.

Compare the strings: print -1 if the first string is less than the second one, 1 if the second string is less, or 0 if they are equal.
inputSpecificationHtml: Each of the first two lines contains a string. The lengths of the strings range from $1$ to $100$ inclusive. It is guaranteed that the strings are of the same length and also consist of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters.
outputSpecificationHtml: If the first string is less than the second string, print -1. If the second string is less than the first string, print 1. If the strings are equal, print 0. Note that the letters' case is not taken into consideration when the strings are compared.
sampleNotesHtml: Convert both strings to lowercase. Compare character by character.
hints: Convert both strings to lowercase first so letter casing is ignored.
Compare them using standard string comparison (< and >).
Return '-1', '1', or '0' accordingly.
explanation: Convert both strings to lowercase with `.toLowerCase()`. Compare using standard lexicographical comparison.

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: Equal Strings (Different Case)
testCases.description: Official sample: 'aaaa' and 'aaaA' are equal ignoring case.

testCases.title: Single Characters Differing in Case
testCases.description: Single char 'Z' vs 'a': lowercase 'z' is greater than 'a'.

testCases.title: Identical Strings
testCases.description: Both strings have identical case and characters.

title: Beautiful Matrix
descriptionHtml:
You've got a $5 \times 5$ matrix, consisting of 24 zeroes and a single number one. Let's index the matrix rows by numbers from 1 to 5 from top to bottom, let's index the matrix columns by numbers from 1 to 5 from left to right.

In one move, you are allowed to apply one of the two following transformations to the matrix:

  1. Swap two neighboring matrix rows, that is, rows with indexes $i$ and $i + 1$ for some integer $i$ ($1 \le i < 5$).
  2. Swap two neighboring matrix columns, that is, columns with indexes $j$ and $j + 1$ for some integer $j$ ($1 \le j < 5$).

You think that a matrix looks beautiful, if the single number one of the matrix is in the middle of it (in the cell that is on the intersection of the third row and the third column). Count the minimum number of moves needed to make the matrix beautiful.
inputSpecificationHtml: The input consists of five lines, each line contains five integers: the $j$-th integer in the $i$-th line of the input represents the element of the matrix that is located on the intersection of the $i$-th row and the $j$-th column. It is guaranteed that the matrix consists of 24 zeroes and a single number one.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the minimum number of moves needed to make the matrix beautiful.
sampleNotesHtml: The target position is $(3, 3)$. The minimum moves is the Manhattan distance: $|r - 3| + |c - 3|$.
hints: Find the coordinates (row, col) of the number 1 (using 1-based indexing, from 1 to 5).
The center of the 5x5 matrix is at row 3, column 3.
Swapping adjacent rows changes row coordinate by 1; swapping adjacent columns changes col by 1.
The total moves needed is the Manhattan distance: abs(row - 3) + abs(col - 3).
explanation: Locate the coordinates $(r, c)$ of the element equal to 1. Moving adjacent rows/cols translates to Manhattan distance to the center $(3, 3)$, which equals $|r - 3| + |c - 3|$.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: Already at Center (3, 3)
testCases.description: Official sample 2: 1 is at center, 0 moves required.

title: Helpful Maths
descriptionHtml:
Xenia is a beginner mathematician. Today the teacher wrote the sum of numbers 1, 2 and 3 on the board. The sum consisted of several numbers and signs "+".

Xenia has just begun learning counting, so she can only calculate a sum if the summands follow in non-decreasing order. For example, she can't calculate a sum $1+3+2+1$ but she can calculate sums $1+1+2$ and $3+3$.

You've got the sum that was written on the board. Rearrange the summands and print the sum in such a way that Xenia can calculate the sum.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains a non-empty string $s$ — the sum Xenia needs to count. String $s$ contains no spaces. It only contains digits and characters "+". The length of string $s$ cannot exceed $100$ characters.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print the new sum that Xenia can count.
sampleNotesHtml: Extract all numbers, sort them ascending, and join them back with '+'.
hints: Split the input string by '+' to get an array of number strings.
Sort the numbers in ascending order.
Join the array back with '+' as the separator.
explanation: Split the string along '+', convert or sort the digits ascendingly, and join them back with '+'.

testCases.title: Sample Test 3: Single Number 2
testCases.description: Official sample with only one summand.

testCases.title: Already Sorted
testCases.description: Expression that is already in non-decreasing order.

title: Stones on the Table
descriptionHtml: There are $n$ stones on the table in a row, each of them can be red, green or blue. Count the minimum number of stones to take from the table so that any two neighboring stones had different colors. Stones of the same color are considered neighboring if there are no other stones between them.
inputSpecificationHtml:
The first line contains integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 50$) — the number of stones on the table.

The next line contains string $s$, which represents the colors of the stones. We'll consider the stones in the row numbered from 1 to $n$ from left to right. Then the $i$-th character $s$ equals "R", if the $i$-th stone is red, "G", if it's green and "B", if it's blue.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the minimum number of stones you need to remove.
sampleNotesHtml: Whenever $s[i] == s[i-1]$, we must remove one stone. So count all adjacent pairs with identical colors.
hints: Any adjacent pair of identical colors violates the rule.
Iterate from index 1 to n - 1.
If s[i] === s[i - 1], increment the count.
explanation: Two adjacent stones with the same color require at least one removal. Therefore, the minimum removals required is simply the count of indices $i$ where $s[i] == s[i-1]$.

testCases.title: Sample Test 3: BRBG
testCases.description: Official sample: no two adjacent have the same color.

title: Boy or Girl
descriptionHtml:
Those days, many boys use beautiful girls' photos as avatars in forums. So it is very hard to tell the gender of a user at the first glance.

Here is a method: if the number of distinct characters in one's user name is odd, then he is a male, otherwise she is a female.

You are given the string that denotes the user name, please help our hero to determine the gender of this user by his method.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains a non-empty string, that contains only lowercase English letters — the user name. The string doesn't contain more than $100$ letters.
outputSpecificationHtml: If the user is a female by our hero's method, print CHAT WITH HER!. If the user is a male, print IGNORE HIM!.
sampleNotesHtml: Count the distinct characters using a Set. If size is even: "CHAT WITH HER!". If odd: "IGNORE HIM!".
hints: Use a Set or frequency array to count the number of unique characters.
Check whether `distinctCount % 2 === 0`.
Even -> 'CHAT WITH HER!', Odd -> 'IGNORE HIM!'.
explanation: Insert all characters into a Set to filter duplicates. Check the parity of the set size: even corresponds to female ('CHAT WITH HER!'), odd to male ('IGNORE HIM!').

testCases.title: Sample Test 1: wjmzbmr (6 distinct letters)
testCases.description: Official sample: {w, j, m, z, b, r} has 6 letters (even).

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: xiaodao (5 distinct letters)
testCases.description: Official sample: {x, i, a, o, d} has 5 letters (odd).

title: Wrong Subtraction
descriptionHtml:
Little girl Tanya is learning how to decrease a number by one, but she does it wrong with a number consisting of two or more digits. Tanya subtracts one from a number by the following algorithm:

  • if the last digit of the number is non-zero, she decreases the number by one;
  • if the last digit of the number is zero, she divides the number by 10 (i.e. removes the last digit).

You are given two integer numbers $n$ and $k$. Tanya will subtract one from $n$ $k$ times. Your task is to print the result after all $k$ subtractions.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line of the input contains two integer numbers $n$ and $k$ ($2 \le n \le 10^9$, $1 \le k \le 50$) — the initial number and the number of subtractions.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print one integer number — the result of the decreasing $n$ by one $k$ times.
sampleNotesHtml: 512 -> 511 -> 510 -> 51 -> 50. Total 4 steps for 512 with k=4 results in 50.
hints: Simulate k steps in a loop.
Check the last digit: if n % 10 === 0, divide by 10 (Math.floor(n / 10)).
Otherwise, subtract 1 (n--).
explanation: Loop $k$ times. In each iteration, if $n$ ends with a zero ($n \% 10 == 0$), integer divide $n$ by 10. Otherwise, decrease $n$ by 1.

testCases.title: Sample Test 2: 1000000000 with 9 steps
testCases.description: Official sample 2: nine zero divisions removes all 9 zeroes, leaving 1.

title: Soldier and Bananas
descriptionHtml:
A soldier wants to buy $w$ bananas in the shop. He has to pay $k$ dollars for the first banana, $2k$ dollars for the second one and so on (in other words, he has to pay $i \cdot k$ dollars for the $i$-th banana).

He has $n$ dollars. How many dollars does he have to borrow from his friend soldier to buy $w$ bananas?
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains three positive integers $k, n, w$ ($1 \le k, w \le 1000$, $0 \le n \le 10^9$) — the cost of the first banana, initial number of dollars the soldier has and number of bananas he wants.
outputSpecificationHtml: Output one integer — the amount of dollars that the soldier must borrow from his friend. If he doesn't have to borrow money, output 0.
sampleNotesHtml: Total cost is $k \times (1 + 2 + \dots + w) = k \times \frac{w(w+1)}{2}$. Borrow amount is $\max(0, \text{totalCost} - n)$.
hints: The sum of numbers from 1 to w is w * (w + 1) / 2.
The total cost is k * w * (w + 1) / 2.
If the soldier has enough dollars (n >= totalCost), he borrows 0. Output max(0, totalCost - n).
explanation: The total cost of $w$ bananas is $k \cdot \sum_{i=1}^w i = k \cdot \frac{w(w+1)}{2}$. The borrowed amount is $\max(0, \text{total} - n)$.

testCases.title: Exact Amount: No Borrowing
testCases.description: Soldier has exactly enough money -> borrows 0.

testCases.title: Zero Initial Dollars
testCases.description: Soldier has 0 dollars -> must borrow entire cost.

testCases.title: Large Number of Bananas
testCases.description: k=1, n=50, w=10 -> cost is 55, borrows 5.

title: Tram
descriptionHtml: Linear tram route has $n$ stops. At each stop $i$, $a_i$ passengers get off and $b_i$ passengers get on the tram. Find the minimum possible tram capacity such that the number of passengers inside never exceeds capacity.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains an integer $n$ ($2 \le n \le 1000$). The next $n$ lines contain pairs of integers $a_i$ and $b_i$ ($0 \le a_i, b_i \le 1000$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the minimum capacity of the tram.
sampleNotesHtml: At the 2nd stop, 2 people exit and 5 enter, giving 6 people in the tram, which is the maximum throughout the route.
hints: Maintain a running passenger counter starting from 0.
At each stop: current = current - a_i + b_i.
Track the maximum value of current throughout the simulation.
explanation: Simulate the passenger count stop by stop. Since the tram starts empty, count = 0. For each stop i, subtract exiting passengers a_i and add entering passengers b_i. The required capacity is max(count) across all stops.

testCases.title: Sample 3: 3 stops constant 1
testCases.description: One person swaps at middle stop.

title: Word
descriptionHtml: Vasya is very upset because he often mixes up uppercase and lowercase letters. Given a word $s$, change the case so that either all letters are lowercase or all are uppercase. Choose the case that requires the minimum changes. If the counts are equal, prefer lowercase.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains word $s$, consisting of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters ($1 \le |s| \le 100$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print the corrected word $s$.
sampleNotesHtml: In HoUse, 2 uppercase and 3 lowercase, so convert all to lowercase: house.
hints: Count uppercase letters and lowercase letters.
If uppercase > lowercase, convert entire string to uppercase.
Else (lowercase >= uppercase), convert entire string to lowercase.
explanation: Loop through the string and count how many characters are uppercase vs lowercase. If uppercase count is strictly greater than lowercase count, convert all characters to uppercase. Otherwise, convert to lowercase.

title: Young Physicist
descriptionHtml: A body is at rest if the vector sum of all forces applied to it equals zero. Given $n$ force vectors $(x_i, y_i, z_i)$, determine whether the body is in static equilibrium.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains an integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 100$). The next $n$ lines each contain three integers $x_i, y_i, z_i$ ($-100 \le x_i, y_i, z_i \le 100$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print YES if the body is in equilibrium, otherwise print NO.
sampleNotesHtml: Check sum(x) == 0 && sum(y) == 0 && sum(z) == 0.
hints: Keep three separate accumulators: sumX, sumY, sumZ.
For equilibrium, ALL THREE sums must equal zero simultaneously.
explanation: Add up all the x coordinates, y coordinates, and z coordinates independently. If sumX == 0 and sumY == 0 and sumZ == 0, output YES, otherwise output NO.

testCases.title: Sample 1: Unequal forces
testCases.description: Vector sum does not equal zero.

testCases.title: Sample 2: Equilibrium forces
testCases.description: Vector sums equal zero on all 3 axes.

title: Queue at the School
descriptionHtml: During recess children stand in a queue. If a boy is standing immediately before a girl, he will let the girl swap positions with him in one second. Given queue string and time $t$, determine the queue state after $t$ seconds.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains integers $n$ and $t$ ($1 \le n, t \le 50$). The second line contains string $s$ of length $n$ with characters B (boy) and G (girl).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print the string representing the queue after $t$ seconds.
sampleNotesHtml: In 1 second, BG turns into GB.
hints: Simulate t rounds.
In each round, iterate through the string and whenever s[i] == "B" and s[i+1] == "G", swap them and skip the next index so you don"t move the boy twice in one second.
explanation: For each second from 1 to t, traverse the string. Whenever you encounter s[i] == "B" and s[i+1] == "G", swap them to s[i] = "G" and s[i+1] = "B", then increment i by 1 extra to avoid moving the same child again in the same second.

testCases.title: Sample 3: All girls and one boy at end

title: Twins
descriptionHtml: You have $n$ coins with values $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$. Find the minimum number of coins to take such that the total sum of your coins is strictly greater than the sum of the remaining coins.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 100$). The second line contains $n$ integers $a_i$ ($1 \le a_i \le 100$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print the minimum number of coins needed.
sampleNotesHtml: Taking coins 3 and 3 gives sum 6 > 0 (taking 1 coin gives 3 which is not strictly greater than 3).
hints: Calculate total sum of all coins.
Sort the coins in descending order.
Greedily pick the largest coin until your accumulated sum > total / 2.
explanation: To minimize the count of coins taken while maximizing their sum, greedily choose the largest values first. Sort the array in non-increasing order. Keep taking coins until your sum strictly exceeds half the total sum.

testCases.title: Sample 1: Two equal coins
testCases.description: Must take both coins for strictly greater sum.

title: Pangram
descriptionHtml: A word or a sentence in some language is called a pangram if all the characters of the alphabet of this language appear in it at least once. Given a string, determine whether it is a pangram.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains an integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 100$). The second line contains string $s$ consisting of uppercase and lowercase Latin letters.
outputSpecificationHtml: Print YES if the string is a pangram, otherwise print NO.
sampleNotesHtml: There are 26 letters in the English alphabet.
hints: Convert the string to lowercase.
Collect all unique letters in a set.
If the set size is 26, it is a pangram.
explanation: Convert the string to lowercase and insert all letters into a set (or boolean frequency array of size 26). If the set has size 26, answer YES, otherwise NO.

title: Kefa and First Steps
descriptionHtml: Kefa wants to celebrate his first progress in competitive programming. Given an array of $n$ numbers, find the length of the maximum non-decreasing contiguous subsegment.
inputSpecificationHtml: The first line contains integer $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$). The second line contains $n$ integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ ($1 \le a_i \le 10^9$).
outputSpecificationHtml: Print a single integer — the maximum length of a non-decreasing contiguous subsegment.
sampleNotesHtml: Subsegment [1, 3, 4] has length 3 and is non-decreasing.
hints: Maintain curLen = 1 and maxLen = 1.
Iterate from index 1 to n-1: if a[i] >= a[i-1], curLen++, else curLen = 1.
Update maxLen = max(maxLen, curLen).
explanation: Loop through the array starting from the second element. If the current number is greater than or equal to the previous number, increment the current streak length. Otherwise, reset the streak length to 1. The answer is the maximum streak encountered.
